nagoya_restaurant_perouges.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Transcribed from the shop's own 公式 (shop-managed) Tabelog menu, 更新日 2026/07/02; all tax-inclusive, no service charge. NOTE: the domain perouges.nagoya has lapsed and now serves a domain-parking page — the shop's live channels are its Instagram and Facebook.

items.note: The everyday lunch: amuse-bouche, one starter, a fish dish, a meat dish, dessert of the day, coffee/tea and petits fours. Booking is compulsory and you choose your course when you book, so tell them about allergies then — they say same-day requests often can't be met. Classical French means flour in the bread, sauces and pastry, so wheat unless arranged in advance.

items.ja: Menu Dejeuner "B"（お昼のフルコース）
items.note: Same shape as A but with a second starter inserted — typically a risotto or a seafood plate. The extra ¥1,000 buys one more course, which is the best-value step up on this menu. Wheat is present in the bread and pastry work; ask when booking.

items.ja: 前日までのご予約限定特別コース "C"
items.romaji: Zenjitsu made no goyoyaku gentei tokubetsu kosu C
items.en: Special course C — must be booked at least a day ahead
items.note: The big lunch: amuse, three starters, fish, meat, TWO desserts, coffee and petits fours. Only bookable by the previous day. Worth it if you want the kitchen's full range at lunch prices. Wheat throughout unless you flag it at booking.

items.ja: Menu du jour（平日限定コース）
items.note: Weekdays only. Amuse, starter, second starter, fish, meat, dessert, coffee and petits fours — the cheapest way into the evening kitchen. Everything is made in house down to the bread and the petits fours, so wheat is unavoidable without notice.

The flagship: amuse, three starters, fish, meat, two desserts, coffee and petits fours. Built on Aichi organic/no-spray vegetables, fish and meat bought at market each morning, and European imports. Reservation-only; the chef will work around dislikes and allergies if told in advance.

items.ja: パーティープラン（120分フリードリンク付き）7品
items.en: Party plan — 7 plates with 120 min free drinks, whole floor to yourselves
items.note: For 10–16 people (they advertise from 8), lunch or dinner, tax included. One floor of the machiya is given over to your group. Good to know if you are travelling with a group and want the food without per-drink arithmetic.

items.ja: パーティープラン（120分フリードリンク付き）8品
items.en: Party plan — 8 plates with 120 min free drinks
items.note: The longer party menu, same 10–16 people and same free-drink window. Tax included and no service charge, which is unusual at this level in Nagoya.
Children are welcome (babies through primary age) and there is a proper kids' course. Prams are fine but usually get seated on the 2nd floor. Contents aren't published — ask when booking.
The shop specialises in natural/low-intervention wine and has a sommelier on the floor; they also allow drinks brought in. Wine is normally gluten-free, but fining agents mean vegans should ask.

items.ja: 冷製ラタトゥユとマグロ、生ハムのサラダ　ポーチドエッグ添え
items.romaji: Reisei ratatouille to maguro, namahamu no sarada, pochido eggu-zoe
items.en: Chilled ratatouille with tuna and prosciutto, poached egg
items.section: コース内の一品（例）Example course dish
items.note: Printed on the shop's own menu as an example of the lunch starter. Cold Provençal vegetable stew used as a bed for raw tuna and cured ham, with a poached egg broken over it. No flour in the dish itself, but it arrives with bread — decline the bread if you're avoiding wheat.

items.ja: サンマとモンサンミッシェルムール貝のリゾット
items.romaji: Sanma to Mon-San-Misheru murugai no rizotto
items.en: Risotto of Pacific saury and Mont-Saint-Michel mussels
items.section: コース内の一品（例）Example course dish
items.note: Listed as an example of the second starter on Menu Dejeuner B. Autumn sanma — the oily silver fish that means autumn in Japan — folded into a rice risotto with French bay mussels. Rice-based, so the likeliest flour-free plate on the menu, but the stock and finishing butter need checking.

items.ja: スズキのポアレ　根セロリのピュレとバルサミコソース
items.romaji: Suzuki no poare, ne-serori no pyure to barusamiko sosu
items.en: Pan-seared sea bass, celeriac puree, balsamic sauce
items.section: コース内の一品（例）Example course dish
items.note: The example fish course. Suzuki (Japanese sea bass) cooked skin-down until crisp, on a puree of celery root with a reduced balsamic sauce. Sauces in this kind of kitchen are usually reductions rather than roux-thickened — worth confirming if wheat matters to you.

items.ja: アイチ鴨のコンフィと白隠元豆のガルビュール
items.romaji: Aichi-gamo no konfi to shiro-ingenmame no garubyuru
items.en: Confit of Aichi duck with white bean garbure
items.section: コース内の一品（例）Example course dish
items.note: One of two example main courses. Local Aichi duck leg salted and slow-cooked in its own fat, served with garbure — the thick white-bean and cabbage soup-stew of south-west France. The most 'French countryside' thing on the card.

items.ja: ハッピーポークのパテのシューファルシー　マデラ酒の香り
items.romaji: Happi poku no pate no shu-farushi, madera-shu no kaori
items.en: Stuffed cabbage of 'Happy Pork' pate, scented with Madeira
items.section: コース内の一品（例）Example course dish
items.note: The alternative main. Pork pate wrapped in cabbage leaves and braised, finished with Madeira — chou farci, French home cooking done seriously. 'Happy Pork' is a branded Japanese pork. Pate commonly carries breadcrumb or flour as a binder, so ask.

nagoya_rakuichi.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Transcribed from a clear photograph of the shop's own laminated menu card, photographed 2026/07. The same card photographed 2026/04 ran ¥100 lower on every bowl, so this is a freshly raised price list. NOTE: the shop writes its name 楽いち and romanises it TANO-ICHI on the menu cover — not 'Rakuichi'.

items.en: 'Tanoichi flavour' — the house light tonkotsu ramen
items.note: Marked おすすめ (the recommendation) and described on the card as 当店自慢の、あっさり豚骨ラーメン — 'our pride, a light pork-bone ramen'. Not the heavy Hakata style: the broth is pork bone simmered clean and peppery, with thin straight noodles, chashu, menma and spring onion. Regulars order it ねぎ増し辛みそ — extra onion with the free chilli miso. Wheat noodles, so not gluten-free.

A made-up word: ちょっと (a bit) crossed with こってり (rich, unctuous). The card explains it as 香味油で、こってりさせたラーメン — the same broth finished with aromatic oil to give it body and gloss. Order this if the standard bowl sounds too restrained. Wheat noodles.

Not the fish of the same name. The card says 沖縄の島唐辛子を使用、キレのある辛いラーメン — built on Okinawan shima-togarashi, the small ferocious island chilli, for a sharp clean heat rather than a dull burn. The hottest thing here. Wheat noodles.

Headed on the card ボリューム満点！汁なしラーメン — 'seriously filling, soupless ramen'. Thick noodles over tare, minced meat and aromatics that you stir hard yourself before eating. Nagoya invented this genre (台湾まぜそば). Wheat noodles and a wheat-soy tare.
The mazesoba with Japanese curry in place of the usual tare. Japanese curry roux is made with wheat flour, so this is wheat twice over. Filling and messy in the best way.

items.ja: まぜそば大盛（1.5倍）／麺ダブル
items.note: +¥150 for 1.5x noodles, +¥300 for double. Applies to the mazesoba only — say 大盛 (omori) or 麺ダブル (men daburu) when you order.

¥50 off when ordered with a ramen. Plain white rice with nothing on it is one of the few things in a ramen shop with no wheat in it — but this is a ten-seat counter where noodles are boiled a metre away, so treat the scoop and the counter as shared, and ask for it unseasoned.

¥50 off with a ramen. Rice under chopped chashu, the pork belly braised in the shop's soy-and-mirin tare — so the sauce is wheat soy even though the rice isn't. Reviewers order it as the lunch-set partner to a bowl.

items.section: ラーメンのみ Ramen only
items.note: ¥100 off the listed price for a smaller bowl. Soup ramen only, not the mazesoba. Useful if you want a rice bowl as well.

items.section: ラーメンのみ Ramen only
items.note: Soup ramen only. Wheat noodles.

items.en: Second helping of noodles into your leftover broth
items.section: ラーメンのみ Ramen only
items.note: The Hakata custom, and the card even reminds you: スープは残しておいてね！ — 'save some soup!'. Order it while you still have broth left and a fresh nest of noodles goes straight into your bowl.

items.en: Two eggs beaten into the soup
items.section: ラーメンのみ Ramen only
items.note: The card notes 玉子を2コ使用、スープがマイルドになります — two whole eggs stirred through, which rounds off the pork-bone edge and thickens the broth. A good move on the chilli 島味.

Free — the card prints it at 0円. A spoonful of chilli-spiked miso stirred into the bowl; the standard local order here is the house ramen with extra onion and this. Miso can be barley-based and the paste often carries soy sauce, so it is not a gluten dodge.
Works on both the soup ramen and the mazesoba, and it is the most-ordered topping here — raw white onion cuts the pork fat. Vegan in itself, but it lands in a non-vegan bowl.
Lacto-fermented bamboo shoot, seasoned; almost always simmered in soy sauce, so wheat unless proven otherwise.
The card promises 中はトロトロ、半熟玉子です — the yolk still running. The marinade is soy-based, so wheat.

items.ja: とろけるチャーシュー増し（2枚）
items.en: Two extra slices of melting chashu
items.note: 'Melting' is the shop's own word for it. Two more slices of the soy-braised pork belly, and the card specifies 2枚. Wheat soy in the braise.
Marked 夜のみ — evenings only, not at lunch. Wheat wrappers plus a soy dipping sauce; there is no gluten-free version of this.

items.ja: おつまみチャーシュー
items.en: A plate of chashu to drink with
items.note: The braised pork on its own instead of on a bowl — the classic ramen-shop drinking snack. Soy-braised, so wheat.

items.en: A dish of seasoned bamboo shoot
items.note: The same menma as the topping, served as a beer snack. Soy in the seasoning is the usual case.
Shredded raw cabbage with dressing — the cheap palate-cleanser you see on counters all over Japan. The dressing is the unknown; sesame and soy-based dressings are the norm.

A block of chilled tofu with toppings. The tofu itself is fine; it is normally crowned with bonito flakes and dressed with soy sauce at the table, which is where both the wheat and the fish come in — ask for it plain.

items.ja: アサヒスーパードライ（中ビン）
items.note: The only beer on the card. Barley beer, so not gluten-free.

¥600 a glass, ¥4,000 for a bottle kept behind the counter. Add 水＆氷 (water and ice) ¥500 per person or 炭酸 (soda) ¥250. Ask for 芋 (imo, sweet potato) rather than 麦 (mugi, barley) if you avoid gluten grains — distillation removes gluten protein, but the barley origin still bothers some coeliacs.

items.ja: ノンアルコールビール
items.note: Still made from malted barley, so alcohol-free is not gluten-free. One-cup sake is ¥600 if you'd rather.

nagoya_osteria_olmo.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Courses from the shop's own site (current). À la carte transcribed from a photograph of OLMO's own printed card, 2025/06 — and read the header before you order: 表記はお二人様分（3名様は×1.5、4名様は×2の金額となります）, i.e. every à la carte price below is for TWO people sharing, ×1.5 for three, ×2 for four, plus 10% consumption tax and 10% service. The card changes constantly — the 2025/01 card shared not one dish with this one.

items.en: 'Stagione' — the chef's full seasonal tasting menu
items.note: Tax and service on top. Described on the shop's own site as 旬の食材を少しずつ、おまかせのフルコース — a little of everything in season, entirely the chef's choice. Booking required, and they specifically ask you to give allergies and dislikes in as much detail as possible AT booking, because same-day requests can't be handled. That advance channel is your only real route to a wheat-free evening here.

items.en: 'Pasta corso' — one starter, four pastas, dessert
items.note: Tax and service on top, must be booked by the day before. One antipasto, then four of the chef's pasta dishes back to back, then dolce — built for people who came for the hand-rolled pasta. Every shape here is wheat pasta, so this course is wheat by definition.

items.ja: 鎌倉 LatteriaBeBè ストラッチャテッラチーズと枇杷のカプレーゼ
items.romaji: Kamakura LatteriaBeBe sutoratchatera chizu to biwa no kapureze
items.en: Caprese of stracciatella from LatteriaBeBe, Kamakura, with loquat
items.note: Stracciatella is the shredded, cream-soaked interior of burrata; this one comes from a Kamakura dairy. Paired with biwa (loquat) instead of tomato — the small apricot-coloured early-summer fruit. No wheat in the dish itself, but bread comes with it.

items.ja: 新潟 メジマグロとビーツのタルタル 赤海苔とキャビア
items.romaji: Niigata mejimaguro to bitsu no tarutaru, aka-nori to kyabia
items.en: Tartare of young bluefin tuna and beetroot, red nori and caviar
items.note: Mejimaguro is juvenile bluefin — leaner and sweeter than the adult fish. Chopped raw with beetroot, then finished with red seaweed and caviar. Raw fish and no flour, but check the seasoning for soy sauce.

items.ja: 三河 縞鰺のバルセートマリネ フルーツトマトのケッカソース
items.romaji: Mikawa shimaaji no barusetto marine, furutsu tomato no kekka sosu
items.en: Mikawa striped jack marinated in balsamic, fruit-tomato salsa cruda
items.note: Shimaaji (striped jack) from Mikawa Bay, an hour from Nagoya — one of the finest white fish in Japan. Cured briefly in aged balsamic and served under salsa alla checca, the uncooked tomato-and-basil sauce. Balsamic occasionally carries caramel or wheat traces; ask.

items.ja: 三河わたり蟹と土佐文旦の冷製 根セロリのサラダ
items.romaji: Mikawa watarigani to Tosa buntan no reisei, ne-serori no sarada
items.en: Chilled Mikawa blue swimmer crab with Tosa pomelo, celeriac salad
items.note: Watarigani is the blue swimming crab; buntan a big fragrant Kochi pomelo. Cold, sweet and citrus-sharp, with celery root for crunch. Naturally flour-free.

items.ja: 熊本県 馬肉のタルタル パルミジャーノ トリュフ
items.romaji: Kumamoto-ken baniku no tarutaru, parumijano, toryufu
items.en: Kumamoto horse tartare, Parmigiano and truffle
items.note: Kumamoto is Japan's horse-meat capital and basashi (raw horse) is eaten there the way beef tartare is in Europe. OLMO treats it as an Italian tartare with parmesan and shaved truffle. Raw, rich, and much milder than it sounds. Tartare is sometimes bound with breadcrumb — confirm.

items.ja: 炭焼きトリッパとペコリーノチーズのインサラータ
items.romaji: Sumiyaki torippa to pekorino chizu no insarata
items.note: The cheapest thing on the card and a good way in. Tripe here is grilled over charcoal rather than stewed Roman-style, then tossed with sharp sheep's cheese and leaves.

items.ja: 三河 子持ちシャコとヤングコーンのフリット
items.romaji: Mikawa komochi shako to yangu kon no furitto
items.en: Fritto of roe-bearing mantis shrimp and baby corn
items.note: Shako is mantis shrimp — sweeter and more mineral than prawn; 子持ち means it is carrying roe, the prized spring state. Fried in batter, so wheat.

items.ja: サザエとマッシュルームのアンチョビソテー 春香うど
items.romaji: Sazae to masshurumu no anchobi sote, harukaka udo
items.en: Turban shell and mushroom sauteed with anchovy, spring udo
items.note: Sazae is the spiral turban shell prised out and cooked — chewy, briny, faintly bitter. Udo is a pale mountain vegetable with a celery-meets-fennel snap that marks early spring in Japan. Anchovy carries no wheat, but check the pan.

items.ja: 勝浦 金目鯛の天火焼き ンドゥイヤソース
items.romaji: Katsuura kinmedai no tenpiyaki, ndouiya sosu
items.en: Oven-roasted Katsuura splendid alfonsino with 'nduja sauce
items.note: Kinmedai is the scarlet, big-eyed deep-water fish landed at Katsuura in Chiba — fatty, sweet, expensive. Roasted and sauced with 'nduja, the spreadable chilli salami of Calabria. A very OLMO move: Japanese fish, Calabrian heat.

items.ja: 三河 赤烏賊の炙り焼きとアーティチョークのユダヤ風
items.romaji: Mikawa akaika no aburiyaki to atichoku no yudaya-fu
items.en: Seared Mikawa red squid with Jewish-style artichoke
items.note: Carciofi alla giudia is the Roman Jewish quarter's twice-fried artichoke, opened out like a flower and eaten leaf and all. Served here against squid flashed over flame. Deep-fried, but traditionally without batter.

items.ja: 白ミル貝の炭火焼きと蚕豆 自家製からすみ
items.romaji: Shiro-mirugai no sumibiyaki to soramame, jikasei karasumi
items.en: Charcoal-grilled white geoduck with broad beans and house bottarga
items.note: Mirugai is the geoduck clam — sweet, crisp, slightly saline. Karasumi is salted, pressed and dried mullet roe, one of Japan's three great delicacies, and OLMO cures its own; it is grated over the top like a fishy parmesan.

items.ja: 焼き鮎 水菜 ピゼリのトンナレッリ 鮎肝コンフィ
items.romaji: Yaki-ayu, mizuna, pizeri no tonnarerri, ayu-kimo konfi
items.en: Tonnarelli with grilled ayu, mizuna and peas, confit ayu liver
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Ayu, the sweetfish, is THE river fish of the Japanese summer — grilled whole over charcoal, faintly melon-scented, and prized for its bitter liver, which here is confited into the sauce. Tonnarelli is square-cut hand-rolled Roman spaghetti. Wheat pasta.

items.ja: カマスと焼き茄子、青唐辛子のタリオリーニ
items.romaji: Kamasu to yaki-nasu, aotogarashi no tariorini
items.en: Tagliolini with barracuda, grilled aubergine and green chilli
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Kamasu (Japanese barracuda) is a lean autumn fish usually salt-grilled; here it goes into a thin ribbon pasta with smoky charred aubergine and fresh green chilli. Wheat pasta.

items.ja: あおり烏賊の墨煮 イカ墨のタリアテッレ
items.romaji: Aoriika no sumini, ikasumi no tariatere
items.en: Squid-ink tagliatelle with bigfin reef squid stewed in its own ink
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Aori-ika is the thick, sweet bigfin reef squid — the best eating squid in Japan. Cooked in its own ink and served on ink-black pasta. It will stain your teeth; that is the point. Wheat pasta.

items.ja: 桜海老と越冬メークイン 丹下農園バジルのジェノベーゼ スパゲッティ
items.romaji: Sakura-ebi to etto mekuin, Tange noen bajiru no jenobeze supagetti
items.en: Genovese spaghetti with sakura shrimp, over-wintered May Queen potato, Tange-farm basil
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Sakura-ebi are tiny translucent pink shrimp landed almost only in Suruga Bay and eaten whole. Pesto genovese classically contains potato, and these are 'over-wintered' May Queens, sweeter for having been stored through the cold. Wheat pasta, and pesto normally has cheese.

items.ja: 日間賀島 真蛸とラディッキオ スパゲッティ プッタネスカ
items.romaji: Himakajima madako to radikkio, supagetti puttanesuka
items.en: Puttanesca with Himakajima octopus and radicchio
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Himakajima is the little octopus island in Mikawa Bay that Nagoya people take the ferry to for tako and fugu. Puttanesca means tomato, olives, capers, anchovy and chilli — the anchovy makes it non-vegetarian. Wheat pasta.

items.ja: 仏 フレッシュモリーユ茸とカステルマーニョのタヤリン サマートリュフ
items.romaji: Furansu furesshu moriyu-take to Kasuterumanyo no tayarin, sama toryufu
items.en: Tajarin with fresh French morels, Castelmagno cheese and summer truffle
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Tajarin is Piedmont's egg-yolk-rich thread pasta, traditionally 30-plus yolks to the kilo. With fresh morels, the crumbly Piedmontese DOP cheese Castelmagno and shaved summer truffle — the most straightforwardly Italian and most luxurious plate on the card. Wheat and egg.

items.ja: いろいろ魚介のジャスミンライスリゾット
items.romaji: Iroiro gyokai no jasumin raisu rizotto
items.en: Mixed seafood risotto made with jasmine rice
items.section: Pasta Risotto パスタ・リゾット
items.note: Rice, not pasta — and Thai jasmine rice rather than Italian carnaroli, which gives a looser, perfumed result. The most plausible wheat-free plate in this section, but the stock, the finishing butter and a kitchen full of pasta flour all need clearing with the chef first.

items.ja: 名古屋コーチンと西浦あさりのココット焼き
items.romaji: Nagoya kochin to Nishiura asari no kokotto-yaki
items.en: Nagoya Cochin chicken and Nishiura clams baked in a cocotte
items.note: Nagoya Cochin is the city's own heritage chicken breed — firmer, darker and far more flavourful than commodity chicken, and a genuine local speciality. Cooked in a lidded pot with asari clams from Nishiura on Mikawa Bay, so the meat steams in clam liquor. The cheapest main and the most 'Nagoya' thing OLMO does.

items.ja: 京都府 弥栄より 40日飼育七谷鴨むね肉（1枚）
items.romaji: Kyoto-fu Iyasaka yori yonjunichi shiiku Nanatani-gamo muneniku
items.en: Breast of 40-day Nanatani duck from Iyasaka, Kyoto (one whole breast)
items.note: Nanatani duck is a small hand-raised Kyoto flock that top kaiseki houses compete for; 40 days is the rearing period. Priced per whole breast. The leg version, spice-confited, is ¥6,000 for two legs. Ask whether the sauce is flour-thickened.

items.ja: 京都中勢以より 熟成但馬牛
items.en: Dry-aged Tajima beef from Nakasei, Kyoto
items.note: The top plate. Tajima is the Hyogo bloodline all Kobe beef descends from; Nakasei is the Kyoto butcher famous for long dry-ageing, which concentrates the meat rather than melting it into softness. Remember this price is for two.

items.ja: OLMOの出来立てティラミス
items.note: Dolce prices are the exception on this card — they are marked ＊お一人様分, per person. 出来立て means assembled when you order rather than set in a tray. Savoiardi biscuits mean wheat, plus raw egg and mascarpone.

items.ja: 本日のジェラート（バニラ／オレンジ／くるみ／ピスタチオ／ヨーグルト）
items.en: Gelato of the day — vanilla, orange, walnut, pistachio, yoghurt
items.note: From ¥500, per person, and the cheapest thing in the building. Made in house; a fruit sorbet is the likeliest wheat-free finish, but it is scooped in a kitchen full of pasta flour, and all but possibly the orange are dairy-based.

nagoya_nayaten.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Nayaten publishes NO menu anywhere reachable: no own site, no shop-managed aggregator page (its HotPepper entry is an auto-generated stub) and not one menu photograph on Tabelog. The course below is reconstructed from four dated first-hand accounts that agree on the sequence — Tabelog 2026/03 and 2024/01, Retty 2025/04, and a Nagoya food blog 2024/01. Diners report spending ¥20,000–¥30,000 a head; one 2024 party reported ¥30,000–¥40,000. There is no à la carte.

items.en: The fugu course — the only thing served
items.note: Read this before anything else. Nayaten is a husband-and-wife counter of seven or eight seats in a residential street in Shirakabe; it opens ONLY between the autumn and spring equinoxes (fugu season); and in practice first-timers cannot book. Someone who already goes has to take you, and that person books the whole counter, because every course is served to the entire room at the same moment. No printed menu and no choices — the master decides. Diners report ¥20,000–¥30,000 a head. Unlike most fugu houses there is NO から揚げ (fried fugu) course here; a 2024 regular says so explicitly.

Tessa is normally fugu sliced so thin you can read the plate through it, fanned into a chrysanthemum. Nayaten deliberately refuses that: every reviewer singles out how THICK the slices are here, chewy and concentrated rather than delicate. One regular briefly dips the tessa into the scalding fin sake before eating it. Fugu flesh has no wheat — the ponzu does.

Named by diners as one of the reasons to come — and it is also the wheat in the meal. Ponzu is citrus juice plus SOY SAUCE plus dashi, and Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat unless it is specifically tamari. It arrives with grated daikon and chives and is used for the sashimi, the skin and the hotpot, so anyone avoiding gluten has to ask for the fish plain with salt and citrus instead.

Fugu skin scalded, chilled and cut into strips — gelatinous and springy, a completely different texture from the flesh. One long-time regular says he prefers the びらびらくにゅくにゅ ('flappy, squidgy') skin to the sashimi. Eaten with the same wheat-soy ponzu.

items.en: Fugu milt, served cold and raw
items.note: Shirako is the male fish's milt sac, and fugu shirako is the most expensive version of it in Japan. Nayaten serves it cold and raw, which almost nobody does — diners describe 純白の透き通るような甘さ, a pure-white translucent sweetness, rich but, they insist, not cloying. If you try one thing here, this is it.

The same milt, this time grilled until the outside browns and the inside turns to hot custard — one blogger compares the lobe to a block of tofu and calls it ほわほわ, warm and downy, dissolving on the tongue. Usually just salt, but confirm there is no soy glaze.

The centrepiece. A kombu-dashi pot on the counter into which the master feeds different cuts in his own order and at his own timing — head, collar, belly, fin meat — so you get a tour of the whole animal rather than one texture. Reviewers repeatedly note that he, not you, runs the pot. The broth itself is usually just kombu and water; the wheat is in the ponzu you dip into.

items.ja: 鍋の野菜（春菊・葱・豆腐など）
items.romaji: nabe no yasai (shungiku, negi, tofu nado)
items.en: Hotpot vegetables — chrysanthemum greens, onion, tofu
items.note: Shungiku (garland chrysanthemum leaf) is the classic partner to fugu — faintly bitter and aromatic — and diners here use it deliberately to reset the palate between rich mouthfuls of milt. Also tofu and negi. Clean in themselves; the ponzu is the problem.

items.en: Rice porridge cooked in the hotpot broth
items.note: The finish, and the thing every single reviewer raves about. When the fish is gone the master strains the pot, drops in rice and egg, and what comes back is a bowl of concentrated fugu essence. People order seconds — one blogger's line for it is 三杯目はそっと出し, you ask for the third bowl quietly. Watch for soy sauce going into the pot at this stage.
A small sweet closes the meal; the contents aren't published and change. Unremarkable next to what precedes it, but reviewers confirm it is there.

The drink of the genre and, by consensus, superb here. A dried, roasted fugu tail fin is dropped into scalding sake; the fin gives off a smoky, nutty, faintly marine depth, and the surface is traditionally lit briefly to burn off alcohol. Sake is brewed from rice and koji so there is no wheat — though the roasted fin means it is not vegetarian in spirit. Regulars drink it right through the meal.

nagoya_nihon_ryori_jo.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Courses from the restaurant's own お品書き PDFs for 葉月 (August) and its TableCheck page; prices include 10% consumption tax but a 15% service charge is added on top. Drinks transcribed from a photograph of the restaurant's own printed drinks card, 2025/10. The お品書き is rewritten every month — the stage names below stay the same, the contents do not.

items.note: Tax in, plus 15% service. The August お品書き runs すすぎ・前菜・椀盛り・お向・追向・焼肴・鉢物・お食事・甘味. It is おまかせ — no choices — and the restaurant asks for allergies AT BOOKING because it cannot adapt once you arrive. Seatings are simultaneous: 11:30 for tables, 12:00 for the counter, and arriving late means you may simply miss courses.

items.en: Special course 'Kyorakumi' — nine stages with an extra opener
items.note: Tax in, plus 15% service. Same shape as the ¥15,000 but with 先付 added ahead of the 前菜 and, at this price, quite different materials. The restaurant's own August PDF files this structure as the 夜席 (evening course) while its TableCheck page also offers it at lunch, so it is bookable at either sitting. Dinner seatings are 18:00 (tables) and 18:30 (counter).

items.en: 'Dine in a yukata' plan — lunch plus a yukata you keep
items.note: Tax in, service extra; summer only (advertised 1 Jul–31 Aug). Includes a full yukata with obi and geta, professional dressing at the hotel, lunch in the restaurant — and you take the yukata home. Arrive an hour before the sitting to be dressed. Add-ons are priced separately (hair ornament ¥1,800, kanzashi/flower ¥2,280, obijime ¥3,000, lace tabi ¥1,800). No children's yukata.

An unusual opener and a signature of the Gion Sasaki school this kitchen is modelled on: a tiny first mouthful whose job is to clear and prepare the palate rather than to impress. Head chef Isao Nagata came via the Aichi Expo state-guest kitchen and two Nagoya Castle Japanese restaurants before opening this room in October 2025.

items.en: Course stage — the amuse (¥30,000 course only)
items.note: The seasonal appetiser that opens a kaiseki proper. It appears only on the ¥30,000 course. Almost always seasoned with dashi and soy sauce, so assume wheat unless you have arranged otherwise in advance.

A composed plate or tiered box of several small seasonal bites — the visual set-piece of the meal, arranged to state which month you are in. Many separate seasonings, so many separate wheat and dashi risks.

items.en: Course stage — the lidded soup bowl
items.note: The dish a kaiseki chef is actually judged on. A lacquered lidded bowl holding clear dashi with one main item, one supporting one and an aromatic garnish. Lift the lid and smell it before you drink. Built on bonito-and-kombu dashi so not vegan, and usually a light usukuchi soy, so wheat.
Literally 'the far side' — the sashimi course, placed at the top of the tray. Raw fish carries no wheat; the soy sauce it is dipped in does. Ask for salt or citrus instead if that matters to you.

items.en: Course stage — a second sashimi (¥15,000 lunch only)
items.note: A follow-up sashimi, usually a contrasting fish or a different cut of the same one. Present on the ¥15,000 lunch お品書き but not on the ¥30,000 one, which spends its extra course on the 先付 instead.

Grilled fish or meat, either salt-grilled (塩焼き) or glazed (照り焼き / 幽庵焼き). The salt-grilled version is one of the very few plates in a kaiseki that can be genuinely wheat-free; anything glazed is soy and mirin, so wheat. Worth asking which you are getting.
A more substantial dish served in a bowl rather than on a plate — simmered, steamed or occasionally fried. If it is fried it is wheat batter; if it is simmered it is dashi and soy.

items.en: Course stage — rice, soup and pickles
items.note: The rice course that formally ends the savoury meal: seasonal rice (often takikomi-gohan cooked with the month's ingredient), miso soup and pickles. Plain rice is clean, but takikomi rice is cooked IN soy-seasoned stock and miso can be barley-based — both are worth raising at booking.

A Japanese-style sweet to close: fruit, a jelly, or a wagashi with matcha. Wagashi are usually rice flour and azuki bean rather than wheat, which makes this one of the safer stages — but not a guarantee.

Two private rooms, up to six people each. ¥10,000 at lunch and ¥20,000 at dinner, on top of the food and the 15% service. Under-10s are not seated at the tables at all — families with small children are put in a private room, so factor the charge in.

items.ja: サントリー マスターズドリーム
items.note: The only beer on the card — Suntory's premium all-malt lager. Malted barley, so not gluten-free.

Suntory's light grain whisky from the Chita distillery on the peninsula just south of Nagoya — a local pour and the gentlest of the three. Made from grain (usually corn); distillation removes gluten protein, but strict coeliacs often avoid grain whiskies anyway.
The forest distillery in the Southern Alps — green, faintly smoky, the classic highball malt. Malted barley base.
Japan's oldest malt distillery, between Kyoto and Osaka; sherry-cask depth, and genuinely hard to find abroad at this price. Malted barley base.
A Kagoshima sweet-potato shochu whose name means 'plough on fine days, read on rainy ones'. Soft and clean; drink it cut with hot water (お湯割り) alongside the course.

One of the cult '3M' sweet-potato shochu from Kagoshima, sold at home by lottery and traded for many times list price. Round, floral, almost sweet. The most expensive pour on the card by a distance, and the reason it is on it.

items.ja: ビットブルガー（ノンアルコールビール）
items.note: German de-alcoholised pilsner. Still brewed from malted barley, so alcohol-free is not gluten-free.

items.ja: デュックドモンターニュ（ノンアルスパークリング）
items.en: Duc de Montagne alcohol-free sparkling wine
items.note: A Belgian de-alcoholised sparkler, dry enough to open a kaiseki with — the obvious choice if you want a toast without drinking.

items.ja: ロイヤルブルーティー 京都宇治碾茶 The Uji
items.romaji: Roiyaru Buru Ti – Kyoto Uji tencha 'The Uji'
items.en: Royal Blue Tea — Uji tencha, bottled cold-brew tea
items.note: Royal Blue Tea bottles cold-brewed leaf tea and sells it like wine, poured from the bottle into a glass and paired course by course. This is the top of the list: tencha, the shaded Uji leaf that matcha is ground from, brewed rather than powdered — deep umami, almost broth-like, and a genuinely convincing alternative to sake with a kaiseki. Tea leaves and water only, no wheat. Two others are ¥3,000 each: フォールインラブ and ジュエル オブ フラワーズ花.

items.ja: 奥会津金山 天然水／天然炭酸水
items.en: Oku-Aizu Kaneyama still / naturally sparkling mineral water
items.note: From Kaneyama in the Oku-Aizu mountains of Fukushima, one of the very few naturally carbonated springs in Japan — the fizz is geological, not added. Water only, so clean on every count; the price is a hotel price.

nagoya_obanzai_afuro.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Transcribed in full from the shop's own handwritten daily おしながき, photographed 2026/06 and dated 6/22 (Monday). THE LIST IS REWRITTEN EVERY DAY — a sheet from 9/2 the previous year shared only about a third of these dishes — so treat this as the shape and the price band (¥400–¥900 a plate) rather than a fixed menu. Drink prices from the shop's printed card photographed 2025/09.

items.note: Strips of cured jellyfish — all crunch, almost no flavour of its own — dressed with umeboshi paste for a sharp salty-sour hit. A classic 'first thing with the first beer' plate. The dressing usually contains soy sauce and dashi, so ask.
Diced raw octopus in a sticky green wasabi dressing — hot enough to hit the back of the nose, and one of the great sake snacks. Almost always seasoned with soy sauce and mirin.

Thumb-sized squid from Toyama Bay that glow blue at sea, cured whole and raw. You eat the whole thing including the ink sac, which is the rich bitter part. Okizuke means 'cured out at sea' — and the curing liquid IS soy sauce, so this is wheat by definition.

The Kyoto benchmark dish and the fastest way to judge an obanzai kitchen: egg beaten with a lot of dashi and rolled layer on layer in a rectangular pan, so it comes out barely set and weeps when cut. Served with grated daikon. Contains bonito dashi and usually a splash of light soy.
The joke of the menu — the little smiley-face potato shapes Japanese kids get at school lunch, deep fried and served to grown-ups with beer. Coated in wheat batter and fried in shared oil.
A whole butterflied aji, breaded in panko and deep fried — the great cheap Japanese fish dish, eaten with tonkatsu sauce and mustard. Panko is wheat bread, so no.

Sticks of gobo — the long earthy root that tastes faintly of soil and artichoke — marinated, dusted and fried until they crisp up like chips. Addictive. Kara-age means a flour/starch dusting, normally with wheat flour in the mix, plus a soy marinade.
The winter twin of hiyayakko: a block of tofu warmed through instead of chilled, buried under boiled baby whitebait. Soft, plain, comforting. Dressed with soy sauce at the table — ask for it without.

The mid-section of the wing — two thin bones, easy to strip with your teeth. Nagoya's own tebasaki tradition means the local version is flour-dusted, fried twice and glazed with sweet soy and a heavy hit of pepper. Wheat in the dusting and the glaze.

items.en: Fish-cake tubes fried in seaweed batter
items.note: Chikuwa is a tube of grilled surimi; isobe-age means fried in a tempura batter mixed with powdered aonori seaweed, which turns it green and gives it a shoreline smell. Pub food, and very good with beer. Wheat batter, and chikuwa itself often contains wheat starch.

The quietest thing on the sheet and a genuine obanzai staple: spinach blanched, squeezed, cut into batons and left to sit in seasoned dashi, served cold with bonito flakes. The steeping liquid is dashi plus soy sauce (so wheat) and the dashi is bonito (so not vegan) — worth asking on both.

The most expensive plate on the sheet and the one to order if you want something substantial. Cubes of belly simmered for hours in soy, sake, mirin and sugar until the fat turns translucent and a chopstick goes through. Soy-braised, so wheat.

items.ja: しらすたまごチャーハン
items.en: Fried rice with whitebait and egg
items.note: Marked with a ★ on the sheet — the shop's own pick. Whitebait and scrambled egg through fried rice; a shime, the carb you order to close the night. Fried rice is normally finished with a splash of soy sauce round the edge of the wok, which is where the wheat comes in.
The heartier of the two closing rice dishes. Same soy-sauce caveat as the whitebait version.

Aubergine and minced pork in the Sichuan-derived chilli-bean sauce, softened for Japanese tastes. The aubergine drinks the oil and goes silky. Doubanjiang (broad-bean chilli paste) is usually fermented with wheat, and there is soy sauce as well.

items.en: Grilled Manganji pepper steeped in dashi
items.note: The most authentically Kyoto plate here. Manganji togarashi is a long, thin-walled Kyoto heirloom pepper — sweet, not hot — charred whole over flame and then dropped into dashi to soak up the liquid, eaten cold. The steeping liquid is dashi plus soy sauce, so ask on both wheat and bonito.

Green peppers cooked whole — uncut, stem and seeds left in — in seasoned stock until they collapse. A very obanzai piece of thrift: nothing thrown away, nothing hurried. The simmering liquid means dashi and soy.

items.ja: ブロッコリー明太マヨ
items.en: Broccoli with spicy cod roe mayonnaise
items.note: Mentaiko is pollock roe cured with chilli — a Fukuoka speciality that Japan now puts on everything — loosened with mayonnaise into a pink dressing for blanched broccoli. Salty, creamy, faintly hot. Mentaiko cures usually contain soy sauce and sake.

Okinawa's national dish: bitter melon in half-moons stir-fried with firm tofu, egg and pork, showered with bonito flakes. Genuinely bitter — that is the point, and it is meant as a summer tonic. Seasoned with soy sauce; contains egg, pork and fish.

items.en: Yellowtail collar and trimmings simmered in soy
items.note: 'Ara' is everything left after the fillets are cut — collar, cheek, bones — and on a fatty winter buri that is the best-eating part of the fish. Simmered hard in soy, sake, mirin, sugar and ginger. Fiddly, cheap, delicious. Soy-braised, so wheat.

Exactly what it says, grilled until the bacon crisps. A staple of every Japanese izakaya rather than anything Kyoto — proof this is a neighbourhood bar as much as an obanzai house. Japanese bacon cures often include soy or wheat-derived seasoning.

items.en: Chinese cabbage in soy-milk tantan broth
items.note: Napa cabbage stewed in a mild soy-milk version of tantan — sesame paste, chilli oil, a little heat — which comes out creamy rather than fiery. Comfort food. Usually built on doubanjiang and soy sauce (wheat) and commonly has minced pork in it, so ask on both counts.

items.ja: 鮭とほうれん草クリーム
items.note: The yoshoku (Japanese-Western) corner of the sheet — salmon and spinach in a cream sauce, eaten with the same chopsticks as the ohitashi next to it. Cream sauces in Japan are frequently thickened with a wheat-flour roux, so ask.

items.ja: 生ビール（サッポロ黒ラベル／アサヒスーパードライ）
items.en: Draught beer — Sapporo Black Label or Asahi Super Dry
items.note: Both on tap at the same price. Barley beer, so not gluten-free. Also on the card: umeshu (plum wine) ¥650 with your choice of rocks, water or soda; house wine ¥2,500 a bottle; soft drinks ¥350–¥450.

items.ja: 日本酒（竹葉・八海山・小左衛門 夏吟・城陽）
items.en: Sake by the glass — four labels
items.note: 竹葉 Chikuha ¥900 (Noto, Ishikawa — dry, made for seafood), 八海山 Hakkaisan ¥850 (Niigata — the clean restrained benchmark), 小左衛門 夏吟 Kozaemon Natsugin ¥950 (Gifu, a summer-only ginjo) and 城陽 Joyo ¥850 (Kyoto). A short, deliberate list, and the Kyoto bottle is the one to drink with the obanzai. Sake is rice, water and koji — no wheat — though a few brewers use a barley-derived enzyme, so a strict coeliac should still ask.
